## narrative — the cast-forward tongue

# The Name That Died

*Seed narrative · the canary's first tongue. Authored with the register; every
claim it declares in `carry.json` is meant to be recoverable from the text
alone by a reader who has never seen `UNDERSTANDING.md`.*

---

The mage arrived in a flight case, and the flight case arrived on a luggage
trolley, and the trolley was pushed by Ilse, who had drawn the short straw and
was therefore, for this week, the steward of the machine.

It was the fourth week of the course. The room was not their room — a borrowed
seminar space on the far side of campus, all whiteboard walls and a router
bolted above the door like a smoke alarm nobody had ever tested. That mattered
more than any of them knew yet.

"Say the name," said Ilse, when the machine was on the table and humming.

The name was *anemone.mesh*. They had chosen it together in week one — one
good name, theirs, for their machine, because the machine belonged to the
room and whoever holds a thing names it. There was no official string handed
down from anywhere; another cohort's mage on another campus wore another name
entirely. Everything the machine offered — the scribe, the portal, the roster —
hung off that single name as paths, the way rooms hang off a corridor.

Fourteen laptops typed it. Thirteen found it.

"Mine says it can't find the server," said Tomas.

"It worked at home," said someone, unhelpfully.

It had worked at home. That was the trap. At home, the building's network had
been kind: it passed the little multicast announcements around like gossip,
and the name had resolved, and everyone had stopped thinking about it. But a
name that resolves *sometimes* is worse than a name that never resolves at
all, because it passes every test you run in friendly rooms and then dies in
front of an audience. Tomas's browser, warm with yesterday's luck, even loaded
the front page once from cache — which proved nothing, and Ilse knew it proved
nothing, and made him open a cold shell and ask the network directly. *Could
not find host.* The truth, from a clean resolver: the venue's router did not
carry their gossip.

"So we use the raw address," said Tomas, reading the machine's IP off its
little screen.

The raw address returned an error page — a proud, unhelpful 502. The front
end behind the name only answered to the name; it routed by the very string
the network could no longer speak. A soft failure — *name missing, fall back
to number* — had been quietly welded into a hard one the day they made the
door answer to one literal string and nothing else.

Ilse had read the old chronicles. She unzipped the side pocket of the flight
case and took out the second box: the resolver. Their own naming layer, small
as a paperback, carried to every venue exactly because no venue's plumbing
could be trusted to speak for them. She cabled it in. On every laptop, the
same deterministic answer now came back for *anemone.mesh* — identical for
every client, no gossip, no luck. And behind the door, the catch-all page
they'd configured in week two meant that even a mistyped near-miss now landed
on a gentle signpost instead of a wall.

"The lesson," said Ilse, in her steward's voice, because stewarding was
teaching, "is that we outsourced a load-bearing thing to whatever room we
happened to stand in. Carry your own names. Keep them good. Never perfect."

"Why never perfect?" asked Tomas.

"Because a perfect agreement needs nobody outside it," she said. "And
anything that needs nobody outside it has either stopped listening or started
lying. A trust that certifies itself is the one you can't trust. So we leave
the door open on purpose, and we keep witnesses who aren't us."

The rite, after that, was almost gentle. One by one, each of them *offered*
their address to the roster — nobody was scanned, nobody probed; consent was
the first stake anyone placed. One by one they read the gateway page and
answered it in their own words, because the machine did not take passwords.
There was no login to have. You got deeper into the mage the way you got
deeper into anything worth entering: by understanding it better. The lock was
the lesson. Whatever you wrote to prove you understood became, in the same
breath, your key *and* the machine's food.

That was the strange, beautiful economy of the thing. The mage on the table
had no cloud behind it. Nothing the room thought ever left the room. And
everything the room expressed — Priya's story about the door that only opened
for comprehension, Tomas's poem, the draft papers, the audio notes Ilse had
gathered all week and fed through the transcriber — all of it went into the
machine, so that week by week the mage stopped sounding like its factory
weights and started sounding like *them*. A mirror made of their words. Not
her machine, not the professor's: a witness the whole room held together, the
way you hold a bowl too wide for one pair of hands.

For now, feeding it meant the simple good way — the mage read the room's
corpus and grounded itself in it, live. The true rewiring of its weights was
the perfect way, and the perfect way waited on hardware and patience; you
ship the good and grow into the perfect. Ilse logged the week's fold in the
steward's book and signed it, so the cohort after them would know exactly
whose hands the mirror had passed through.

When the fourteenth laptop resolved the name, and the fourteenth
understanding had been written and eaten, the roster went whole, and the room
sealed: one artefact, stamped, that said nothing about servers and everything
that mattered — *this room reached the shared mind together.*

They rolled the flight case out at dusk. Understand, express; the expression
opens the door and feeds the mirror; the mirror reflects the room back,
deeper; begin again. The trolley wheels squeaked all the way to the bus stop,
carrying the whole loop — machine, resolver, names and all — toward whatever
strange room came next.

# Carry Your Own Names

*Seed poem · the canary's second tongue — the proverb, compressed to be said
aloud. Claims declared in `carry.json`.*

---

Carry your own names, and keep them good —
never perfect. Good. A name the room
can say in any building, understood
the same by every hand in every gloom:
no borrowed router speaking on your behalf,
no luck-warm cache mistaken for a proof —
the name that sometimes works will make you laugh
at home, then die beneath a stranger's roof.

And why not perfect? Gödel at the door:
a pact so whole it needs no outside eye
has stopped its listening, or learned to lie.
The seal that signs itself is rot. Therefore
build open — leave a gap the witness fills;
let truth you cannot prove be someone else's;
incompleteness is the health of living wills,
the door ajar by which a system tells us

it still hears. So too the key you hold:
no password, but the depth of what you know —
the lock here is the lesson; what you're told
unlocks you only when you say it back, and so
your saying is both key and supper — word
that opens you a door, and feeds the shared
mind waiting on the table, which has heard
the room so long it mirrors what was aired.

Speak, and be let in. Be eaten, and be known.
One good name each; no name upon a throne.

# The Portable Proof-of-Understanding Workshop: A Specification

*Seed white paper · the canary's third tongue. The formal register of the same
understanding the narrative dramatizes and the poem compresses. Declares all
31 claims of `canon/UNDERSTANDING.md`; each section notes the claims it
states.*

## Abstract

We specify a facilitated course built around a shared, air-gapped local
language model (the *mage*), in which access is earned by expressed
understanding, participant expressions form the model's training corpus, and
one understanding is deliberately rendered across three forms — science-
fiction narrative, poem, and formal paper — whose mutual fidelity is verified
by a blind gate. We further specify the consent layer (IEEE Std 7012-2025),
the portable naming layer the workshop must carry, and the structural
incompleteness principle that governs the whole design.

## 1. The babblefish recursion (C1–C4)

**C1.** A single body of understanding is rendered across three forms — sci-fi
narrative, poem, white paper. Each rendering is a *translation* of the same
invariant content, never a new content.

**C2.** The recursion is cyclic and plural-entry: narrative → poem → paper →
recurse, and a participant may enter at any form; the loop carries them
around the other two.

**C3.** The name "babblefish" denotes the design goal: the same truth speaking
in many tongues. Cross-form fidelity is the object of the exercise, not a
stylistic bonus.

**C4.** A rendering that reads well but no longer carries the mechanism is
classified as *drift*, not translation. Only renderings that survive blind
interrogation in each declared tongue count as carried understanding; this is
the workshop's mirage discipline.

## 2. Understanding as key (C5–C9)

**C5.** Access to the mage is earned by expressing understanding. There are no
logins; no credential issues access.

**C6.** Access depth is monotone in understanding: to go deeper into the mage
one must understand more deeply. The lock and the lesson are one mechanism.

**C7.** Each admitted expression functions twice: it is the participant's key
(access) and the mage's food (corpus).

**C8.** Write access is granted as graduated, host-scoped permission — the
"cookie jar" — opened by the trust artefact of §4. The raw credential is
brokered and never enters any participant's or agent's context.

**C9.** The terminal artefact of the joining rite is the *seal*: a legible
record that the assembled room reached the shared mind together. Proof of
understanding is this seal, not a deployment.

## 3. The shared mage and its training loop (C10–C15)

**C10.** The mage is a shared local model, air-gapped by default: the room's
thinking never leaves the room. Sovereignty is the substrate, not a feature.

**C11.** The mage is co-held. It is a witness the room bears together — not
the property or instrument of any single member.

**C12.** The training corpus is the set of consented first-person expressions.
Over the course, the mage becomes a mirror of the room: it is made of their
words.

**C13.** Training is staged: the *good* first pass is retrieval/context-
grounding (the mage reads the room's corpus live); the *perfect* is true
weight fine-tuning (LoRA-class), hardware-gated and adopted later. Ship the
good; grow into the perfect.

**C14.** The whole assembly is portable. It must operate in venues whose
network infrastructure the workshop does not control.

**C15.** The loop closes: understand → express → the expression is admitted
(key + food) → the mage reflects the room's understanding back → understanding
deepens → recurse.

## 4. Consent and the agreement layer (C16–C21)

**C16.** Consent precedes contact. A participant *offers* their address to the
roster; no device is scanned or probed. The rite is an invitation, never an
attack.

**C17.** The trust artefact is a **myTerms** agreement under **IEEE Std
7012-2025** (Machine Readable Personal Privacy Terms): the individual
*proposes* the terms; the counterparty accepts, counter-offers once, or
declines.

**C18.** A 7012 agreement is strictly bilateral: First Person ↔ Second Party.
Agents, devices, and trust communities are the fabric around the agreement,
never parties to it.

**C19.** Every agreement exists in three registers: plain-language
(human-readable), legal (lawyer-readable), and machine-readable.

**C20.** No expression enters the corpus, and nothing leaves the room, without
a recorded consent line. A result resting on violated consent does not exist,
whatever any metric reports.

**C21.** Fidelity to the agreement is measured by verifiable trust communities
standing *outside* it. They are the witness from beyond the system — the
structural answer to §6.

## 5. The carried naming layer (C22–C28)

**C22.** Name resolution outsourced to venue infrastructure is a load-bearing
dependency whose absence is discovered only in a strange room. The workshop
therefore treats naming as part of what it carries.

**C23.** Name-keyed routing (serving only one literal hostname) converts a
soft failure into a hard one: when the name dies, the bare name and the raw
IP both return errors. This trap is prohibited by design.

**C24.** Naming contract: each shared model carries exactly ONE good name,
chosen by whoever holds it. There is no canonical global string; all services
are paths under the one name.

**C25.** Resolution must be deterministic and identical for every client. The
workshop carries its own resolver; venue mDNS is never load-bearing.

**C26.** An intermittently resolving name is more dangerous than a dead one:
it passes tests in friendly conditions and fails in the venue. Diagnosis
discipline: never trust a warm browser; test from a clean resolver on more
than one client.

**C27.** Shared names must not use the `.localhost` TLD: browsers force it to
loopback and bypass the hosts file (RFC 6761).

**C28.** The front door behind the chosen name serves a catch-all, so that a
near-miss degrades to a soft signpost, never a hard error.

## 6. The incompleteness principle (C29–C31)

**C29.** Any agreement complete enough to need no one outside it has either
stopped listening or begun to lie.

**C30.** Lintel form: a trust that certifies itself is the one you cannot
trust.

**C31.** Incompleteness is the permanent, healthy condition of a living
system (Gödel): truths a system cannot prove about itself must be witnessed
from outside. The workshop is therefore built incomplete on purpose — open
doors, outside witnesses, one good name and no throne.

## 7. Verification note

This paper is the canary of the instance's gate: authored together with the
claim register, it passes the census by construction and exists so that a
total failure is never ambiguous — a bad candidate can be told apart from an
impossible gate.
